Gonorrhea treatment coverage includes data on individuals who identify as transgender or gender diverse, choosing an identity other than male or female. 3. Maintaining data privacy, security, and confidentiality is critical in all reporting processes. 4. The percentage of people diagnosed with a specific sexually transmitted infection (STI) syndrome during the reporting period is measured. 5. This includes the percentage of individuals attending HIV prevention services diagnosed with one of five STI syndromes (urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, genital ulcer disease, anorectal discharge) and the percentage of people living with HIV diagnosed with these syndromes. 6. Diagnosing and treating syndromic STIs improves health outcomes, reduces STI transmission, and contributes to lowering HIV transmission rates. 7. In resource-limited settings, WHO syndromic treatment guidelines remain the standard of care when laboratory diagnosis is unavailable or delayed. 8. WHO 2021 guidelines for managing symptomatic infections address five syndromes: urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, genital ulcer disease, and anorectal discharge. 9. Countries initiating STI syndromic data collection should prioritize urethral discharge, genital ulcer disease, and vaginal discharge syndromes. 10. The numerator is the number of people diagnosed with a specific STI syndrome during the reporting period, disaggregated into those attending HIV prevention services and those living with HIV. 11. The denominator is the total number of people attending HIV prevention or treatment services during the reporting period. 12. Individual-level data from program records is preferred for measurement, but aggregate data can be used if individual data is unavailable. 13. The presence of STI syndromes is a new priority indicator, with disaggregation by gender, age, key populations, HIV status, and geographic regions. 14. Repeat diagnosis of the same STI syndrome within a short period suggests inadequate treatment, untreated partners, or unsafe sexual practices. 15. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) test coverage measures the percentage of individuals tested for HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) during the reporting period, including those attending HIV prevention services, people living with HIV, and pregnant women. 16. Testing pregnant women for HBV is essential for their health and preventing mother-to-child transmission. 17. Knowing HBV testing coverage helps assess antenatal care quality and monitor programmatic targets in countries with HBV vaccination policies. 18. The numerator is the number of people tested for HBsAg during the reporting period, disaggregated by HIV prevention services, people living with HIV, and pregnant women. 19. The denominator is the total number of people attending HIV prevention or treatment services or antenatal care during the reporting period. 20. Measurement relies on patient monitoring tools, such as electronic or paper records, lab registers, and reporting forms. 21. HBV positivity measures the percentage of individuals tested for HBsAg who had a positive result, disaggregated by HIV prevention services, people living with HIV, and pregnant women. 22. Testing for HBV identifies HIV and HBV co-infection, allowing for treatment adjustments to address chronic HBV infection. 23. The HBsAg positivity rate among antenatal care attendees can monitor HBV prevalence and burden in the population. 24. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) test coverage measures the percentage of individuals tested for HCV antibodies, RNA, or core antigen during the reporting period, disaggregated by HIV prevention services and people living with HIV. 25. Testing for HCV co-infection among people living with HIV informs clinicians about the need for further evaluation and treatment adaptation. 26. Disaggregated estimates highlight gaps in diagnosing HCV infection. 27. HCV positivity measures the percentage of individuals tested for HCV who had a positive result, disaggregated by HIV prevention services and people living with HIV. 28. Many people living with HIV and receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) die from liver disease caused by untreated HCV. 29. Testing for HCV among people living with HIV identifies co-infection and allows for treatment adaptation. 30. Highly effective HCV treatments are now available, achieving high virus clearance rates regardless of subtype. 31. HBV treatment among people living with HIV measures the percentage of individuals co-infected with HBV who are on tenofovir-based ART. 32. Tenofovir-based regimens are preferred for treating HIV and HBV co-infection and can be used among people with tuberculosis and pregnant women. 33. HCV treatment among people living with HIV measures the percentage of individuals co-infected with HCV who initiated treatment with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) during the reporting period. 34. Treating HCV among people living with HIV improves quality of life, life expectancy, and reduces mortality. 35. Trends in HCV treatment initiation reflect progress in addressing the disease burden. 36. Disaggregation of data indicates equity in treatment enrollment among priority populations. 37. HCV cure among people living with HIV measures the percentage of individuals co-infected with HCV who completed treatment and achieved sustained virological response (SVR). 38. SVR is assessed by measuring viral load 12–24 weeks after treatment completion. 39. Short courses of HCV treatment with DAAs cure over 90% of patients and reduce mortality. 40. Information on SVR measures treatment effectiveness and provides incentives, such as cure certificates. 41. Cervical cancer screening measures the number of women living with HIV screened for cervical cancer using any test. 42. Progress in scaling up cervical cancer screening among women living with HIV is monitored. 43. Screening intervals depend on the test used, so the number of women screened may vary annually. 44. The numerator is the number of women living with HIV screened for cervical cancer using any test, such as HPV DNA testing, visual inspection with acetic acid, or cytology. 45. Measurement relies on health facility patient registers and records.
